Normalise the inputs, then the activations inside the network, to train faster and more robustly. Then softmax, to classify into more than two classes.

import Section from '../../components/notes/Section.astro'; import Key from '../../components/notes/Key.astro'; import NormalisePanels from '../../components/notes/NormalisePanels.astro'; import BnFlow from '../../components/notes/BnFlow.astro'; import SoftmaxBars from '../../components/notes/SoftmaxBars.astro';
Same notation as in [Deep neural networks](/dataviz/deep-learning/deep-neural-networks), with a few new symbols:
$\mu, \sigma^2$
mean and variance, computed on the training set or on the current mini-batch
$\epsilon$
a tiny number that avoids a division by zero
$\gamma^{[l]}, \beta^{[l]}$
scale and shift of batch normalisation in layer $l$, learned like $W^{[l]}$. Not the $\beta$ of momentum
$C$
number of classes, the size of the output layer: $C = n^{[L]}$
$c_j$
the $j$-th class
Features on very different scales stretch the cost function into a long, thin valley, and gradient descent zigzags across it. Normalised inputs give a rounder cost, and learning goes faster.
$$ \mu = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} x^{(i)} $$ $$ \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \big(x^{(i)} - \mu\big)^2 $$ $$ X := \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} $$

element-wise, one $\mu$ and one $\sigma$ per feature

 Normalise the test set with the same $\mu$ and $\sigma$, those of the training set.
Batch normalisation applies the same idea inside the network, to $z^{[l]}$ in each hidden layer. It makes the network more robust and the search for hyperparameters much easier. For a layer $l$, with $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ computed over the $z^{[l](i)}$ of the current mini-batch: $$ z^{[l](i)}_{norm} = \frac{z^{[l](i)} - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} $$

mean 0 and variance 1 for every unit

 Mean 0 and variance 1 is not always the best distribution for learning. Two new learned parameters let the network pick its own: $$ \begin{aligned} \tilde z^{[l](i)} &= \gamma^{[l]} \, z^{[l](i)}_{norm} + \beta^{[l]} \\[4pt] a^{[l](i)} &= g^{[l]}\big(\tilde z^{[l](i)}\big) \end{aligned} $$ With $\gamma^{[l]} = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}$ and $\beta^{[l]} = \mu$, batch normalisation would give back $z^{[l]}$ unchanged: the network can learn to undo it where it does not help. The bias $b^{[l]}$ is no longer needed: subtracting the mean cancels it, and $\beta^{[l]}$ already shifts the values.
$\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ are computed on each mini-batch. $\gamma^{[l]}$ and $\beta^{[l]}$ are parameters, learned across all the mini-batches. $$ \begin{aligned} & J\big(\ldots, W^{[l]}, \gamma^{[l]}, \beta^{[l]}, \ldots\big) \\[6pt] & \text{gradients } dW^{[l]}, \; d\gamma^{[l]}, \; d\beta^{[l]} \\[6pt] & W^{[l]} := W^{[l]} - \alpha \, dW^{[l]} \\[2pt] & \gamma^{[l]} := \gamma^{[l]} - \alpha \, d\gamma^{[l]} \\[2pt] & \beta^{[l]} := \beta^{[l]} - \alpha \, d\beta^{[l]} \end{aligned} $$

works the same with momentum, RMSprop or Adam
Softmax generalises logistic regression to $C$ classes. The output layer has $C$ units, and the prediction is a probability for each class.
Label, one-hot $$ y^{(i)} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{C \times 1} $$
Prediction $$ \hat y^{(i)} = \begin{bmatrix} \vdots \\ P\big(c_j \mid x^{(i)}\big) \\ \vdots \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{C \times 1} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} z^{[L]} &= W^{[L]} a^{[L-1]} + b^{[L]} \\[4pt] t &= e^{z^{[L]}} \\[4pt] \hat y_j &= \frac{t_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{C} t_k} \end{aligned} $$

$t \in \R^{C \times 1}$, the exponential is element-wise; the $\hat y_j$ are positive and add up to 1
$$ \mathcal{L}(\hat y, y) = -\sum_{j=1}^{C} y_j \log \hat y_j $$

with a one-hot $y$, only the true class counts: $\mathcal{L} = -\log \hat y_{true}$

 With $C = 2$ this is the cross-entropy loss of logistic regression. The cost is the mean over the $m$ examples, as before: $$ J = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathcal{L}\big(\hat y^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\big) $$ Backward propagation starts from a remarkably simple gradient: $$ dz^{[L]} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{[L]}} = \hat y - y $$ ### Why: softmax and log cancel out The derivative of softmax is $\dfrac{\partial \hat y_j}{\partial z_k} = \hat y_j \big(\delta_{jk} - \hat y_k\big)$, with $\delta_{jk} = 1$ if $j = k$ and 0 otherwise. Then:
$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_k} &= -\sum_{j=1}^{C} \frac{y_j}{\hat y_j} \cdot \hat y_j \big(\delta_{jk} - \hat y_k\big) \\[6pt] &= -y_k + \hat y_k \sum_{j=1}^{C} y_j \\[6pt] &= \hat y_k - y_k \end{aligned} $$
The last step uses $\sum_j y_j = 1$, true for a one-hot label.

import Section from '../../components/notes/Section.astro'; import Key from '../../components/notes/Key.astro'; import Figure from '../../components/notes/Figure.astro'; import ActivationCurves from '../../components/notes/ActivationCurves.astro';
$n$
number of input features
$m$
number of training examples
$(i)$
refers to the $i$-th training example
$[l]$
refers to the $l$-th layer of the network
$L$
the output layer, and the number of layers: hidden layers plus the output layer
$\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}$
the $i$-th training example: input features $x$ and labelled output $y$
$\hat y$ or $a$
the prediction: for the same $x$ we want $\hat y \approx y$. Also written $a$, for activation
$g$
activation function
$\{W, b\}$
the model: parameters learned during training
$\alpha$
learning rate
$\lambda$
regularisation parameter
For one training example, vectorised over all the units of layer $l$. The index $(i)$ is left out. $$ z^{[l]} = W^{[l]} \cdot a^{[l-1]} + b^{[l]} \qquad \in \R^{n^{[l]} \times 1} $$ $$ a^{[l]} = g^{[l]}\big(z^{[l]}\big) \qquad \in \R^{n^{[l]} \times 1} $$ Four usual choices for $g$. The dashed curve is the derivative $g'$, which backward propagation needs.
The output layer gives the prediction. It is computed by **forward propagation**. $$ \hat y^{(i)} = a^{[L](i)} \qquad \in \R^{n^{[L]} \times 1} $$
Put the $m$ training examples side by side as columns, and one pass computes the whole training set.
$$ X = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & \mid & & \mid \\ x^{(1)} & x^{(2)} & \cdots & x^{(m)} \\ \mid & \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n \times m} $$ $$ Y = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & \mid & & \mid \\ y^{(1)} & y^{(2)} & \cdots & y^{(m)} \\ \mid & \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n^{[L]} \times m} $$ $$ Z^{[l]} = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & \mid & & \mid \\ z^{[l](1)} & z^{[l](2)} & \cdots & z^{[l](m)} \\ \mid & \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n^{[l]} \times m} $$ $$ A^{[l]} = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & \mid & & \mid \\ a^{[l](1)} & a^{[l](2)} & \cdots & a^{[l](m)} \\ \mid & \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n^{[l]} \times m} $$ $$ B^{[l]} = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & \mid & & \mid \\ b^{[l]} & b^{[l]} & \cdots & b^{[l]} \\ \mid & \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n^{[l]} \times m} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} Z^{[l]} &= W^{[l]} \cdot A^{[l-1]} + B^{[l]} \\[4pt] A^{[l]} &= g^{[l]}\big(Z^{[l]}\big) \end{aligned} $$

with $Z^{[l]}, A^{[l]} \in \R^{n^{[l]} \times m}$
$$ \begin{aligned} & A^{[0]} = X \\[2pt] & \textbf{for } l = 1 \textbf{ to } L \\ & \qquad Z^{[l]} = W^{[l]} \cdot A^{[l-1]} + B^{[l]} \\ & \qquad A^{[l]} = g^{[l]}\big(Z^{[l]}\big) \end{aligned} $$ The last activation, $A^{[L]}$, is the prediction for all the training examples.
The cost is the average of the loss $\mathcal{L}$ over the $m$ training examples. $$ J = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathcal{L}\big(a^{[L](i)}, y^{(i)}\big) $$

$J$ is a function of all the parameters $W^{[1]}, b^{[1]}, \ldots, W^{[L]}, b^{[L]}$

 With the cross-entropy loss, for a binary output: $$ \begin{aligned} J = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \Big[\, & y^{(i)} \log a^{[L](i)} \\ + & \big(1 - y^{(i)}\big) \log\big(1 - a^{[L](i)}\big) \Big] \end{aligned} $$
Notation: for any variable $v$ of the loss, $dv$ is the partial derivative of the loss with respect to $v$. For example: $$ dv = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial v} \qquad\qquad dz^{[l]} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{[l]}} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & dA^{[L]} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^{[L]}}\big(A^{[L]}, Y\big) \\[4pt] & \textbf{for } l = L \textbf{ down to } 1 \\ & \qquad dZ^{[l]} = dA^{[l]} \odot g^{[l]\prime}\big(Z^{[l]}\big) \\[2pt] & \qquad dW^{[l]} = \frac{1}{m}\, dZ^{[l]} \cdot A^{[l-1]T} \\[2pt] & \qquad dB^{[l]} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} dZ^{[l](i)} \\[2pt] & \qquad dA^{[l-1]} = W^{[l]T} \cdot dZ^{[l]} \end{aligned} $$ $\odot$ is the element-wise product. The sum for $dB$ runs over the columns, one per training example. ### Why: the chain rule For one example, with $z^{[l]} = W^{[l]} a^{[l-1]} + b^{[l]}$ and $a^{[l]} = g^{[l]}(z^{[l]})$:
$$ \begin{alignedat}{2} dz^{[l]} &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{[l]}} \cdot \frac{\partial a^{[l]}}{\partial z^{[l]}} &&= da^{[l]} \odot g^{[l]\prime}\big(z^{[l]}\big) \\[10pt] da^{[l-1]} &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{[l]}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{[l]}}{\partial a^{[l-1]}} &&= W^{[l]T} \cdot dz^{[l]} \\[10pt] dW^{[l]} &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{[l]}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{[l]}}{\partial W^{[l]}} &&= dz^{[l]} \cdot a^{[l-1]T} \\[10pt] db^{[l]} &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{[l]}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{[l]}}{\partial b^{[l]}} &&= dz^{[l]} \end{alignedat} $$
Binary classification with a single unit, the smallest neural network. Prediction, loss, cost, gradient descent and L2 regularisation.

import Section from '../../components/notes/Section.astro'; import Key from '../../components/notes/Key.astro'; import SingleUnit from '../../components/notes/SingleUnit.astro'; import LossExplorer from '../../components/notes/LossExplorer.astro';
$n$
number of input features
$m$
number of training examples
$(i)$
refers to the $i$-th training example
$\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}$
the $i$-th training example: input features $x$ and labelled output $y$
$\hat y$ or $a$
the prediction: for the same $x$ we want $\hat y \approx y$. Also written $a$, for activation
$\{w, b\}$
the model: parameters learned during training
$\alpha$
learning rate
$\lambda$
regularisation parameter
For one training example $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}$:
features $$ x^{(i)} \in \R^{n \times 1} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1^{(i)} \\ x_2^{(i)} \\ \vdots \\ x_n^{(i)} \end{bmatrix} $$
weights $$ w \in \R^{n \times 1} = \begin{bmatrix} w_1 \\ w_2 \\ \vdots \\ w_n \end{bmatrix} $$
label $$ y^{(i)} \in \{0, 1\} $$
bias $$ b \in \R $$
For binary classification, the label $y$ is 0 or 1 and the prediction $\hat y$ is the probability that $y = 1$. $$ z^{(i)} = w^T \cdot x^{(i)} + b = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j \, x_j^{(i)} + b $$ $$ a^{(i)} = \hat y^{(i)} = \sigma\big(z^{(i)}\big) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z^{(i)}}} $$
The loss $\mathcal{L}$ measures the error on one training example: we want $\hat y \approx y$. The index $(i)$ is left out. $$ \mathcal{L}(a, y) = -\,y \log a - (1 - y) \log(1 - a) $$ Only one term is left for a given label. If $y = 1$, the loss is $-\log a$, small when $a$ is close to 1. If $y = 0$, it is $-\log(1 - a)$, small when $a$ is close to 0. Move $z$ to see both.
The cost $J$ is the mean of the loss over the whole training set of $m$ examples. $$ J(w, b) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathcal{L}\big(\hat y^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\big) $$ Put the examples side by side as columns, and one pass computes them all.
$$ X = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & \mid & & \mid \\ x^{(1)} & x^{(2)} & \cdots & x^{(m)} \\ \mid & \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n \times m} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} Y &= \begin{bmatrix} y^{(1)} & \cdots & y^{(m)} \end{bmatrix} \\ Z &= \begin{bmatrix} z^{(1)} & \cdots & z^{(m)} \end{bmatrix} \\ A &= \begin{bmatrix} a^{(1)} & \cdots & a^{(m)} \end{bmatrix} \\ B &= \begin{bmatrix} b & \cdots & b \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned} \quad \in \R^{1 \times m} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} Z &= w^T \cdot X + B \\[4pt] A &= \sigma(Z) \\[4pt] J &= -\frac{1}{m}\, \operatorname{sum}\big(Y \odot \log A \\ &\qquad + (1 - Y) \odot \log(1 - A)\big) \end{aligned} $$

$\odot$ is the element-wise product, and sum adds up the $m$ columns
Gradient descent finds the $w$ and $b$ that minimise the cost $J(w, b)$.
  1. 0
    Initialise $w$ and $b$, zeros are fine for a single unit.
  2. Repeat until convergence
    1. 1
      Prediction $A = \sigma(w^T X + B)$ for all the examples.
    2. 2
      Cost $J$, mainly to check that it decreases from one iteration to the next.
    3. 3
      Update the parameters: $$ \begin{aligned} w &:= w - \alpha \, \frac{\partial J}{\partial w}(w, b) \\[4pt] b &:= b - \alpha \, \frac{\partial J}{\partial b}(w, b) \end{aligned} $$
### The partial derivatives The cost is a mean, so its derivative is the mean of the derivatives of the loss: $$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w}(w, b) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{\partial}{\partial w} \mathcal{L}\big(a^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\big) $$ For one example, with $z = w^T x + b$, the chain rule splits each derivative into small parts:
$$ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a}}_{(1)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}}_{(2)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}}_{(3)} $$ $$ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a}}_{(1)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial a}{\partial z}}_{(2)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial z}{\partial b}}_{(4)} $$
$$ \begin{alignedat}{2} &(1) \quad & \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a} &= -\frac{y}{a} + \frac{1 - y}{1 - a} \\[10pt] &(2) & \frac{\partial a}{\partial z} &= \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big) = a(1 - a) \\[10pt] &(3) & \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} &= x \\[10pt] &(4) & \frac{\partial z}{\partial b} &= 1 \end{alignedat} $$
The first two parts simplify nicely: $$ (1) \cdot (2) = -y(1 - a) + (1 - y)\,a = a - y $$
$$ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} = x\,(a - y) \quad \in \R^{n \times 1} $$ $$ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b} = a - y \quad \in \R $$
$$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{m}\, X \cdot (A - Y)^T \quad \in \R^{n \times 1} $$ $$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial b} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \big(a^{(i)} - y^{(i)}\big) $$
Adding regularisation often helps to prevent overfitting. L2 regularisation adds the squared norm of the weights to the cost, so large weights cost more. $$ J(w, b) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathcal{L}\big(\hat y^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\big) + \frac{\lambda}{2m} \lVert w \rVert^2 $$

with $\lVert w \rVert^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j^2$, the squared Euclidean norm

 Each $w_j^2$ derives to $2\,w_j$, so the extra term adds $\frac{\lambda}{m}\,w$ to the gradient. The bias $b$ is not regularised. $$ \frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{m}\, X \cdot (A - Y)^T + \frac{\lambda}{m}\, w \quad \in \R^{n \times 1} $$
Two ways to fight overfitting, L2 and dropout, then four ways to train faster, from mini-batches to Adam.

import Section from '../../components/notes/Section.astro'; import Key from '../../components/notes/Key.astro'; import DropoutNets from '../../components/notes/DropoutNets.astro'; import BatchStrips from '../../components/notes/BatchStrips.astro'; import EwaChart from '../../components/notes/EwaChart.astro';
Same notation as in [Deep neural networks](/dataviz/deep-learning/deep-neural-networks), with a few new symbols:
$\lambda$
regularisation parameter
$keep\_prob$
probability of keeping a unit with dropout
$s$
mini-batch size
$\{k\}$
refers to the $k$-th mini-batch
$t$
iteration, one update step
$\beta_1, \beta_2$
weights of the past in the momentum and RMSprop averages
$\epsilon$
a tiny number that avoids a division by zero
Regularisation reduces overfitting. L2 adds the squared weights of every layer to the cost, so large weights cost more. $$ \begin{aligned} J = & \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathcal{L}\big(a^{[L](i)}, y^{(i)}\big) \\ & + \frac{\lambda}{2m} \sum_{l=1}^{L} \big\lVert W^{[l]} \big\rVert_F^2 \end{aligned} $$

with the squared Frobenius norm $\lVert W^{[l]} \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n^{[l]}} \sum_{j=1}^{n^{[l-1]}} \big(W^{[l]}_{ij}\big)^2$

 If $dW^{[l]}_{BP}$ is the gradient from backward propagation, the extra term adds $\frac{\lambda}{m} W^{[l]}$ to it: $$ dW^{[l]} = dW^{[l]}_{BP} + \frac{\lambda}{m}\, W^{[l]} $$ so the update becomes $W^{[l]} := W^{[l]} - \alpha \big(dW^{[l]}_{BP} + \frac{\lambda}{m} W^{[l]}\big)$, which reads better as: $$ W^{[l]} := \Big(1 - \frac{\alpha \lambda}{m}\Big)\, W^{[l]} - \alpha \, dW^{[l]}_{BP} $$ Each step first shrinks the weights by a factor just below 1, hence the name.
Dropout shuts down some units of the hidden layers at random, a new draw on every training iteration. Each iteration trains a different, smaller network, so no unit can rely on one other unit: it might be gone at the next step. The mask $D^{[l]}$ has the shape of $A^{[l]}$, one column per example. Each entry is 1 with probability $keep\_prob$, and 0 otherwise.
Activations $$ A^{[l]} = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & & \mid \\ a^{[l](1)} & \cdots & a^{[l](m)} \\ \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} $$
Mask $$ D^{[l]} = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & & \mid \\ d^{[l](1)} & \cdots & d^{[l](m)} \\ \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} $$
$$ \begin{aligned} A^{[l]} &:= A^{[l]} \odot D^{[l]} \\[4pt] A^{[l]} &:= A^{[l]} \,/\, keep\_prob \end{aligned} $$

apply the mask, then scale up what is left

 $$ \begin{aligned} dA^{[l]} &:= dA^{[l]} \odot D^{[l]} \\[4pt] dA^{[l]} &:= dA^{[l]} \,/\, keep\_prob \end{aligned} $$

the same mask: the units shut down going forward stay shut going back

 Dividing by $keep\_prob$ keeps the expected value of $A^{[l]}$ unchanged. That is the "inverted" in inverted dropout: nothing changes at test time, when dropout is off.
Batch, mini-batch and stochastic gradient descent differ only in the number of examples used for one update step. **Batch** gradient descent takes a step on all the $m$ examples. **Mini-batch** cuts the training set into mini-batches of $s$ examples, $1 < s < m$, and loops over them. **Stochastic** gradient descent is a mini-batch of one example.
Mini-batch k, inputs $$ X^{\{k\}} = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & & \mid \\ x^{(1)} & \cdots & x^{(s)} \\ \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n \times s} $$
Mini-batch k, labels $$ Y^{\{k\}} = \begin{bmatrix} \mid & & \mid \\ y^{(1)} & \cdots & y^{(s)} \\ \mid & & \mid \end{bmatrix} \in \R^{n^{[L]} \times s} $$
Each step only sees part of the data, so the direction of the update varies: the path to the minimum oscillates. The next three methods smooth it out.
Momentum keeps an exponentially weighted average of the past gradients and steps along that average instead of the raw gradient.
$$ V_t = \beta_1 V_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_1)\, \theta_t $$ $$ V_t^{corr} = \frac{V_t}{1 - \beta_1^{\,t}} $$

$V_0 = 0$, so the first values are too small: the bias correction divides them back up

 Here on real data: a large $\beta_1$ remembers more of the past and gives a smoother, later curve. Turn the bias correction off to see the average start from 0. $$ \begin{aligned} & V_{dW^{[l]}} = \beta_1 V_{dW^{[l]}} + (1 - \beta_1)\, dW^{[l]} \\[2pt] & V_{db^{[l]}} = \beta_1 V_{db^{[l]}} + (1 - \beta_1)\, db^{[l]} \\[6pt] & W^{[l]} := W^{[l]} - \alpha \, V_{dW^{[l]}} \\[2pt] & b^{[l]} := b^{[l]} - \alpha \, V_{db^{[l]}} \end{aligned} $$

$dW^{[l]}$ and $db^{[l]}$ come from backward propagation on the current mini-batch
Root mean square propagation averages the squares of the gradients instead. Dividing by their root slows the steps down in the directions that oscillate the most. $$ \begin{aligned} & S_{dW^{[l]}} = \beta_2 S_{dW^{[l]}} + (1 - \beta_2) \big(dW^{[l]}\big)^2 \\[2pt] & S_{db^{[l]}} = \beta_2 S_{db^{[l]}} + (1 - \beta_2) \big(db^{[l]}\big)^2 \\[8pt] & W^{[l]} := W^{[l]} - \alpha \, \frac{dW^{[l]}}{\sqrt{S_{dW^{[l]}}} + \epsilon} \\[4pt] & b^{[l]} := b^{[l]} - \alpha \, \frac{db^{[l]}}{\sqrt{S_{db^{[l]}}} + \epsilon} \end{aligned} $$

squares, roots and divisions are element-wise
Adaptive moment estimation combines momentum and RMSprop, both with bias correction. $$ \begin{aligned} & V_{dW^{[l]}} = \beta_1 V_{dW^{[l]}} + (1 - \beta_1)\, dW^{[l]} \\[2pt] & S_{dW^{[l]}} = \beta_2 S_{dW^{[l]}} + (1 - \beta_2) \big(dW^{[l]}\big)^2 \\[8pt] & V^{corr}_{dW^{[l]}} = \frac{V_{dW^{[l]}}}{1 - \beta_1^{\,t}} \\[4pt] & S^{corr}_{dW^{[l]}} = \frac{S_{dW^{[l]}}}{1 - \beta_2^{\,t}} \\[8pt] & W^{[l]} := W^{[l]} - \alpha \, \frac{V^{corr}_{dW^{[l]}}}{\sqrt{S^{corr}_{dW^{[l]}}} + \epsilon} \end{aligned} $$

the same for $b^{[l]}$, with $db^{[l]}$

Avoidable bias - train a bigger model - train longer - a better optimisation algorithm: momentum, RMSprop, Adam - another architecture: activation functions, CNN, RNN
Variance - get more data - data augmentation - regularisation: L2, dropout - another architecture: activation functions, CNN, RNN

Overfitting the dev set - get a bigger dev set
For a binary classifier, every prediction falls into one of four boxes: right or wrong, for a positive or a negative. Accuracy alone can mislead when one class is rare: a model that always predicts "negative" scores 99% if only 1% of the samples are positive. Precision, recall and their F1 score tell the real story.
